review: Kantor Gottfried (a church musician in Leipzig, 1735): I am pleased that the voices move with propriety; the melody sits squarely on the beat; the harmonies are such as any good master would write. However, too many phrases simply stop instead of cadencing. The melody is quite memorable – I find myself humming it.

layers.text: The vocal line is played note for note, with the singer's own timing and phrasing.
The original bass line is played exactly, by the double basses and cellos.

Every other part (synths, guitars, keys, pads) is transcribed note for note and given to classical instruments by register: violins, violas, cellos, horns, clarinets, plus pizzicato or harp for short plucked notes.
The drum kit becomes orchestral percussion: kick → timpani (tuned to the chord), snare → concert snare drum, crashes → suspended cymbal.

era.name: Baroque
era.summary: Music built from interweaving lines (counterpoint) over a constantly moving bass, with ornamented melodies and steady, motor-like rhythm.
traits: Counterpoint: several independent melodic lines at once
Basso continuo: a bass line plus harpsichord filling in the chords
Terraced dynamics: whole sections loud or soft, rarely gradual
Ornaments: trills, mordents and decorated long notes
One steady pulse and mood per movement
era.instruments: Strings, harpsichord, organ, recorder/flute, oboe, bassoon, natural trumpet, timpani
why: All three eras were tried. Baroque scored best (Baroque 1.230, Classical 1.161, Romantic 1.155). The score combines how classical it sounds, how much of the song survives, and how well the song suits the composer.
The melody is busy and runs in steady note values, which suits Baroque 'motor' rhythm and running counterpoint.
The energy stays fairly even from verse to chorus, matching Baroque's one-mood-per-piece style.

applied: A walking continuo bass moves under every beat

ensemble.name: Orchestra
ensemble.summary: String sections plus woodwinds, horns or trumpets, timpani (and harp in Romantic style).
why: Near the 'original' end of the slider the full orchestra is used. It is the only classical ensemble with enough colours to cover the vocals, synths, bass and drums at once.
Why it works: the full colour palette: the song's loud choruses can swell into the whole orchestra.
The violins i carries the vocal melody (F#4–B5). It was moved by octaves into the instrument's most singing register, with the key unchanged.

changes.ending: It follows the original beat by beat and lasts exactly as long as the clip (19.1s).
changes.dropped: The drum kit, synths and electric bass are gone. Their rhythmic drive now comes from the accompaniment patterns.
